meta_desc: Mental math for Grade 2: make-ten, add tens then ones, near-doubles and counting up, plus a 10-minute daily routine, a free quiz and printable worksheets.
excerpt: By Grade 2 a child should reach for a strategy before a pencil. Here are the mental math moves I teach, a ten-minute routine that makes them stick, and a quick quiz to check where your child stands.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 2 child to work out 27 + 8 and watch what happens. One reaches for a pencil and starts stacking the numbers in columns. Another looks up at the ceiling for a second and says ‘thirty-five’. Same sum, same age — but the second child has something the first one is still missing: mental math. That is the real Grade 2 goal, and it is exactly what a good set of mental math Grade 2 worksheets is built to train.

In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, the children who move quickly are not the ones with the best memory. They are the ones who know a handful of strategies and know when to use each. Below are the moves that carry Grade 2, the ten-minute routine that makes them automatic, and where paper practice actually earns its place.

What mental math really means in Grade 2

Mental math is not doing sums fast in your head with no method — that is just memory under pressure, and it breaks the moment numbers get bigger. Real mental math is choosing a shortcut that fits the numbers in front of you. A Grade 2 child working with two-digit numbers should be able to add and subtract within 100, spot pairs that make ten, and lean on doubles they already know. NCERT and most school syllabi expect this fluency by the end of the year.

The five strategies that carry Grade 2

1. Make ten to cross a ten

This is the workhorse. To do 27 + 8, borrow 3 from the 8 to lift 27 up to 30, then add the leftover 5: 30 + 5 = 35. It leans on knowing the pairs that make ten (7 and 3 here), which is why bonds to ten are worth drilling until they are instant.

2. Add the tens, then the ones

For 34 + 23, split each number: add the tens (30 + 20 = 50), add the ones (4 + 3 = 7), then put them together for 57. Children find this far friendlier than column addition because they can hold each step in their head. When the ones cross ten — say 38 + 25 — they fold in the make-ten trick: 50, then 8 + 5 = 13, so 63.

3. Near-doubles

Doubles get memorised early and happily. Once a child knows 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 comes free as ‘double 6, plus 1’. The same trick scales: 15 + 16 is double 15 plus 1, which is 31. Teaching a near-double as a doubling plus a nudge beats counting on every time.

4. Subtract by counting up

Here is the counter-intuitive one that surprises most parents: the easiest way to subtract is often to add. For 43 − 38, do not count backwards. Instead count up from 38 to 43 — that is a hop of 5. Children make far fewer mistakes counting up a small gap than counting down a long one, and it quietly builds the link between addition and subtraction.

5. Where the times tables begin

Grade 2 is not about full multiplication tables, but it is where the seeds go in. Skip-counting in 2s, 5s and 10s (2, 4, 6, 8… or 5, 10, 15, 20…) is early multiplication in disguise. A child who can rattle off the 5s is halfway to the five times table before it is ever formally taught.

A ten-minute daily routine that sticks

Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday, every time. The rhythm I recommend to parents in Tier-2 cities who juggle work and school runs is deliberately light:

  • Two minutes of bonds to ten — call out a number, child gives its partner to ten. Instant, no paper.
  • Three minutes on one strategy — pick just one (say make-ten) and do six sums out loud together.
  • Three minutes of skip-counting — count in 2s one day, 5s the next, 10s the third.
  • Two minutes of mixed sums on paper — here the child must choose the strategy, which is where real fluency shows.

That last step matters most. A worksheet that mixes sum types forces the choosing muscle; a page of identical make-ten problems does not. So keep oral drill for building a skill and save written practice for testing whether the child can pick the right tool unprompted.

Why worksheets still earn their place

Oral practice is where a strategy is born, but paper is where it is proven. A printable sheet gives a child a full page to work through at their own pace, and it gives you an answer key so you are not marking sums in your head while cooking dinner. One honest caveat: do not chase speed too early. A child who reasons out 43 − 38 in five seconds by counting up is in a far better place than one who has memorised it but cannot explain why. Speed arrives on its own once the thinking is sound.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Mental Math Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions covering make-ten, adding tens and ones, near-doubles and counting up. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Make ten: take 3 from the 8 to lift 27 to 30, then add the leftover 5. 30 + 5 = 35.
Add the tens (30 + 20 = 50), then the ones (4 + 3 = 7). 50 + 7 = 57.

questions.q: Which is the quickest way to work out 6 + 7?
questions.explanation: 6 + 7 is a near-double: double 6 is 12, and one more makes 13.
Count up from 38 to 43. That is a hop of 5, so the answer is 5.

questions.q: Which number completes the pair to make ten with 3?
questions.explanation: 3 and 7 make ten. Knowing bonds to ten powers the make-ten strategy.

questions.q: What comes next when skip-counting in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, __?
questions.explanation: Skip-counting in fives adds 5 each time, so after 20 comes 25.
Add the tens (30 + 20 = 50). The ones cross ten: 8 + 5 = 13. 50 + 13 = 63.
This is a near-double. Double 15 is 30, and one more makes 31.

faq.q: What mental math should a Grade 2 child know?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 2 a child should add and subtract within 100 in their head using strategies — make-ten, adding tens then ones, near-doubles and counting up — plus skip-count fluently in 2s, 5s and 10s.

faq.q: Is it better to teach mental math or column methods first?
faq.a: Mental strategies first. A child who understands why 34 + 23 is 57 by adding tens and ones will use column methods far more accurately later. The written method should record thinking the child already has, not replace it.

faq.q: How do I help a child who still counts on fingers?
faq.a: Give them a better tool rather than banning fingers. Drill bonds to ten daily until they are instant, then show make-ten. Once the strategy is faster than counting, most children drop the fingers on their own.

faq.q: How much daily practice is enough for Grade 2?
faq.a: About ten focused minutes a day — a mix of quick oral drills and a few written sums — beats one long weekly session. Consistency matters more than length at this age.
